MUJAHID:v1p316#3/r1.author: Mujāhid b. Jabr
MUJAHID:v1p316#3/r1.speaker: مجاهد
MUJAHID:v1p316#3/r1.claim: Mujahid says the truth became clear.

MUQATIL:12:48-51/r4.author: Muqātil b. Sulaymān
MUQATIL:12:48-51/r4.speaker: author
MUQATIL:12:48-51/r4.claim: The women deny knowing any evil of Joseph; Zulaykha then confesses that she pursued him and that he spoke truthfully, as already stated in 12:32.

MUQATIL:12:48-51/r5.author: Muqātil b. Sulaymān
MUQATIL:12:48-51/r5.speaker: author
MUQATIL:12:48-51/r5.claim: Khatb means affair or matter, as in the messengers' question in 15:57; the women had urged Joseph to satisfy Zulaykha, but he refused.

MAJAZ:v1p314/r1.author: Abū ʿUbayda Maʿmar b. al-Muthannā
MAJAZ:v1p314/r1.speaker: author
MAJAZ:v1p314/r1.claim: Al-āna ḥaṣḥaṣa al-ḥaqq means now the truth has become clear and manifest.

ABDURRAZZAQ:v2p324#4/r1.author: ʿAbd al-Razzāq al-Ṣanʿānī
ABDURRAZZAQ:v2p324#4/r1.speaker: قتادة
ABDURRAZZAQ:v2p324#4/r1.claim: Qatada explains حصحص الحق as the truth becoming clear.

AKHFASH:v1p399/r1.author: al-Akhfash al-Awsaṭ
AKHFASH:v1p399/r1.speaker: بعض أهل العلم
AKHFASH:v1p399/r1.claim: Some scholars say all the women tried to seduce Joseph, rather than only the ruler’s wife.

AKHFASH:v1p399/r2.author: al-Akhfash al-Awsaṭ
AKHFASH:v1p399/r2.speaker: author
AKHFASH:v1p399/r2.claim: The plural address راودتن can be used even of one woman, just as الناس can refer to one man in the report about Abu Sufyan.

IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB:v1p218#6/r1.author: Ibn Qutayba
IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB:v1p218#6/r1.speaker: author
IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB:v1p218#6/r1.claim: Khatb means your affair or situation.

IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB:v1p218#6/r2.author: Ibn Qutayba
IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB:v1p218#6/r2.speaker: author
IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB:v1p218#6/r2.claim: Ḥaṣḥaṣ al-ḥaqq means the truth became clear and manifest.

TAB-FULL:v0p213/r1.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v0p213/r1.speaker: السدي
TAB-FULL:v0p213/r1.claim: Al-Suddi relates that the king told the women his information that the Aziz’s wife had pursued Joseph, after which she confessed that the truth had emerged.

TAB-FULL:v0p213/r2.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v0p213/r2.speaker: ابن زيد
TAB-FULL:v0p213/r2.claim: Ibn Zayd glosses حصحص as “became clear.”

TAB-FULL:v0p213/r3.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v0p213/r3.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v0p213/r3.claim: The root ḥaṣṣ means to remove something completely; the reduplicated forms حصحص, كبكب, كفكف, and ذرذر convey the same base action, and here falsehood is cut away so truth appears.

TAB-FULL:v0p213/r4.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v0p213/r4.speaker: ابن إسحاق
TAB-FULL:v0p213/r4.claim: Ibn Ishaq identifies the wife as Ra’il, who says the truth has emerged and Joseph was truthful in his accusation against her.

TAB-FULL:v0p213/r5.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v0p213/r5.speaker: مجاهد
TAB-FULL:v0p213/r5.claim: Mujahid’s gloss is that the truth became clear.

TAB-FULL:v0p213/r6.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v0p213/r6.speaker: قتادة
TAB-FULL:v0p213/r6.claim: Qatada says the truth was now manifest.

TAB-FULL:v0p213/r7.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v0p213/r7.speaker: الضحاك
TAB-FULL:v0p213/r7.claim: Al-Dahhak gives the same gloss: the truth became clear.

TAB-FULL:v13p203#2/r1.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v13p203#2/r1.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v13p203#2/r1.claim: The omitted narrative is that the messenger returned, the king summoned the women and the Aziz’s wife, and asked what had happened when they pursued Joseph.

TAB-FULL:v13p203#2/r2.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v13p203#2/r2.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v13p203#2/r2.claim: The question ما خطبكن means “what was your affair or situation”; the women deny any wrongdoing, and the wife admits she pursued Joseph and affirms his truthfulness.

TAB-FULL:v13p203#2/r3.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v13p203#2/r3.speaker: ابن عباس
TAB-FULL:v13p203#2/r3.claim: Ibn Abbas glosses حصحص الحق as “the truth became clear.”

TAB-FULL:v13p203#2/r4.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v13p203#2/r4.speaker: مجاهد
TAB-FULL:v13p203#2/r4.claim: Mujahid also glosses حصحص الحق as the truth becoming clear.

TAB-FULL:v13p203#2/r5.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v13p203#2/r5.speaker: قتادة
TAB-FULL:v13p203#2/r5.claim: Qatada says that the truth has now become manifest.

ZAJJAJ:v3p115/r1.author: al-Zajjāj
ZAJJAJ:v3p115/r1.speaker: author
ZAJJAJ:v3p115/r1.claim: Joseph did not single out the ruler’s wife, out of good companionship and courtesy; he grouped her with the other women.

ZAJJAJ:v3p115/r2.author: al-Zajjāj
ZAJJAJ:v3p115/r2.speaker: author
ZAJJAJ:v3p115/r2.claim: The readings are ḥāsha li-llāh, ḥāshā li-llāh, and al-Ḥasan’s ḥāsh li-llāh with still shīn; the author rejects the last because consecutive sukūns are not Arabic.

ZAJJAJ:v3p115/r3.author: al-Zajjāj
ZAJJAJ:v3p115/r3.speaker: author
ZAJJAJ:v3p115/r3.claim: Ḥaṣḥaṣa al-ḥaqq means truth emerged and became clear; its root suggests truth’s share or side separating from falsehood.

IBNABIHATIM:v7p2156/r1.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v7p2156/r1.speaker: عبد الرحمن بن زيد بن اسلم
IBNABIHATIM:v7p2156/r1.claim: The king asked the women what had happened when they tried to seduce Joseph; they replied that God forbid, they knew no evil of him.

IBNABIHATIM:v7p2156/r3.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v7p2156/r3.speaker: ابن اسحاق
IBNABIHATIM:v7p2156/r3.claim: The wife of al-Aziz declared that the truth had now become clear.

IBNABIHATIM:v7p2156/r4.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v7p2156/r4.speaker: ابن عباس
IBNABIHATIM:v7p2156/r4.claim: “Now the truth has become clear” means the truth has become manifest.

IBNABIHATIM:v7p2156/r5.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v7p2156/r5.speaker: قتادة
IBNABIHATIM:v7p2156/r5.claim: The truth became manifest, and the wife confessed that she had pursued Joseph and that he was truthful; Hasan exclaimed in condemnation, asking what made her do it.

IBNABIHATIM:v7p2156/r6.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v7p2156/r6.speaker: ابن اسحاق
IBNABIHATIM:v7p2156/r6.claim: “Ḥaṣḥaṣa al-ḥaqq” means that the truth emerged and became clear.

IBNABIHATIM:v7p2156/r7.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v7p2156/r7.speaker: ابن عباس
IBNABIHATIM:v7p2156/r7.claim: In an account of the questioning, the king of Egypt asked whether the women had seduced Joseph, and al-Aziz's wife confessed.

IBNABIHATIM:v7p2156/r8.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v7p2156/r8.speaker: ابن اسحاق
IBNABIHATIM:v7p2156/r8.claim: The wife acknowledges Joseph was truthful about what he had said, after falsely accusing him.

THALABI:v5p229/r2.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v5p229/r2.speaker: author
THALABI:v5p229/r2.claim: The passage omits the messenger’s return and the king’s summoning of the women and Aziz’s wife before asking what happened when they solicited Joseph.

THALABI:v5p229/r3.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v5p229/r3.speaker: author
THALABI:v5p229/r3.claim: The women say hāsha lillāh, meaning God forbid, and deny knowing any evil of Joseph; the Aziz’s wife confesses, and ḥaṣḥaṣ means truth became clear.

THALABI:v5p229/r4.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v5p229/r4.speaker: author
THALABI:v5p229/r4.claim: The verb ḥaṣḥaṣ is related to ḥaṣ, removing something completely; reduplicated forms such as kabkaba, kafkafa, and raddada are cited, with Abu Qays’s poem as evidence.

THALABI:v5p229/r5.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v5p229/r5.speaker: author
THALABI:v5p229/r5.claim: The wife means that falsehood and lying have vanished and truth has appeared; she admits seduction and confirms Joseph’s honesty.

THALABI:v5p229/r6.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v5p229/r6.speaker: author
THALABI:v5p229/r6.claim: Joseph’s ensuing words mean the Aziz should know Joseph did not betray him in his absence; the wife’s confession and Joseph’s statement are joined without naming the speaker transition.

THALABI:v5p229/r7.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v5p229/r7.speaker: author
THALABI:v5p229/r7.claim: The author compares this abrupt linkage of different speakers with the queen’s words in 27:34 and Pharaoh’s words after his council in 26:35.

THALABI:v5p229/r8.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v5p229/r8.speaker: الفراء
THALABI:v5p229/r8.claim: Al-Farra calls this an especially obscure construction: one person’s speech is narrated and another person’s statement follows without a fresh speaker attribution.

MAWARDI-FULL:v3p45#2/r1.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v3p45#2/r1.speaker: author
MAWARDI-FULL:v3p45#2/r1.claim: The women attest to Joseph's innocence based on what they know; testimony to a negative must rest on knowledge, whereas testimony to a positive is categorical, as God's rule for testimony.

MAWARDI-FULL:v3p45#2/r13.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v3p45#2/r13.speaker: author
MAWARDI-FULL:v3p45#2/r13.claim: The king's question publicly assumes Joseph's truthfulness, by God's kindness, discouraging the women from quickly contradicting him.

MAWARDI-FULL:v3p45#2/r14.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v3p45#2/r14.speaker: author
MAWARDI-FULL:v3p45#2/r14.claim: Although the solicitation came only from the wife of al-Aziz, the king may use the plural out of consideration for her and to avoid singling her out.

MAWARDI-FULL:v3p45#2/r15.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v3p45#2/r15.speaker: author
MAWARDI-FULL:v3p45#2/r15.claim: Alternatively, each of the women may have solicited Joseph.

MAWARDI-FULL:v3p45#2/r2.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v3p45#2/r2.speaker: ابن عباس ومجاهد وقتادة
MAWARDI-FULL:v3p45#2/r2.claim: حصحص الحق means the truth has now become clear and manifest.

MAWARDI-FULL:v3p45#2/r3.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v3p45#2/r3.speaker: author
MAWARDI-FULL:v3p45#2/r3.claim: حصحص derives from حص شعره, cutting hair close so the skin appears, and from a حصّة of land cut off; thus truth breaks through and separates from falsehood.

MAWARDI-FULL:v3p45#2/r4.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v3p45#2/r4.speaker: الزجاج
MAWARDI-FULL:v3p45#2/r4.claim: The doubled form حصحص adds intensification, comparable to كبوا and كبكبوا.

MAWARDI-FULL:v3p47/r1.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v3p47/r1.speaker: author
MAWARDI-FULL:v3p47/r1.claim: An unnamed poet uses حصحص الحق for the moment truth becomes clear, as lexical evidence.

MAWARDI-FULL:v3p47/r2.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v3p47/r2.speaker: author
MAWARDI-FULL:v3p47/r2.claim: The wife's unprompted confession displays repentance and confirms Joseph's truth; confession against oneself is stronger than testimony, and God joins testimony with confession to remove doubt.

QUSHAYRI:v2p77/r1.author: al-Qushayrī
QUSHAYRI:v2p77/r1.speaker: author
QUSHAYRI:v2p77/r1.claim: God made the woman’s admission expose the truth after Joseph had been falsely accused and kept in prison.

QUSHAYRI:v2p80/r2.author: al-Qushayrī
QUSHAYRI:v2p80/r2.speaker: author
QUSHAYRI:v2p80/r2.claim: Truth cannot remain hidden forever: God eventually removed the accusation and made Joseph’s innocence clear through his accusers.

QUSHAYRI:v2p80/r3.author: al-Qushayrī
QUSHAYRI:v2p80/r3.speaker: author
QUSHAYRI:v2p80/r3.claim: Because the wife was not yet complete in love, she blamed Joseph; when her love matured, she confessed her own guilt.

QUSHAYRI:v2p80/r4.author: al-Qushayrī
QUSHAYRI:v2p80/r4.speaker: author
QUSHAYRI:v2p80/r4.claim: Complete love leads people to expose themselves and care little whether private matters become public.

QUSHAYRI:v2p80/r5.author: al-Qushayrī
QUSHAYRI:v2p80/r5.speaker: author
QUSHAYRI:v2p80/r5.claim: Joseph spared the women punishment despite their slander, showing the saints’ compassion and willingness to oppose their own interests.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p146#2/r1.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p146#2/r1.speaker: المفسرون
WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p146#2/r1.claim: The king called the women, including the governor's wife, and asked them what had happened.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p146#2/r10.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p146#2/r10.speaker: حميد بن ثور
WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p146#2/r10.claim: Ḥumayd b. Thawr's line uses حصحص of a camel's knees settling on hard gravel.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p146#2/r11.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p146#2/r11.speaker: الزجاج
WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p146#2/r11.claim: Al-Zajjāj derives حصحص from حصة: the share of truth separated from the share of falsehood.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p146#2/r2.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p146#2/r2.speaker: ابن عباس
WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p146#2/r2.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās glosses ما خطبكن as “what is your story?”; others say “what is your affair?”

WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p146#2/r3.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p146#2/r3.speaker: ابن الأنباري
WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p146#2/r3.claim: The king questioned all the women because he had heard that some had solicited Joseph and wanted to identify who did it.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p146#2/r4.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p146#2/r4.speaker: author
WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p146#2/r4.claim: Another possibility is that all the women solicited Joseph: the governor's wife directly, and the others by urging him to comply with her.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p146#2/r5.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p146#2/r5.speaker: ابن عباس
WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p146#2/r5.claim: ما علمنا عليه من سوء means that the women knew of no fornication by Joseph.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p146#2/r6.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p146#2/r6.speaker: الزجاج
WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p146#2/r6.claim: After the women cleared Joseph, the governor's wife said truth had now emerged; Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujāhid, and Qatāda agree.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p146#2/r7.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p146#2/r7.speaker: ابن عباس
WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p146#2/r7.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujāhid, and Qatāda gloss حصحص الحق as the truth becoming clear and manifest.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p146#2/r8.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p146#2/r8.speaker: الفراء
WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p146#2/r8.claim: Al-Farrāʾ says the wife confessed after the women cleared Joseph, fearing they would testify against her if she continued lying.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p146#2/r9.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p146#2/r9.speaker: ابن الأنباري
WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p146#2/r9.claim: Linguists explain حصحص الحق as becoming clear, settled, and firm, comparing it to a camel settling onto the ground and separating the gravel.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p148/r1.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p148/r1.speaker: author
WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p148/r1.claim: The pronoun in “he is among the truthful” refers to Joseph's claim that she had solicited him.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p86#2/r1.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p86#2/r1.speaker: ابن عباس
WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p86#2/r1.claim: The women in the city were women of high standing; al-Wāḥidī finds this most plausible because Zulaykhā invited elite women to her banquet.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p86#2/r2.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p86#2/r2.speaker: الكلبي
WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p86#2/r2.claim: Al-Kalbī identifies four women: wives of the cupbearer, baker, animal handler, and prison keeper.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p86#2/r3.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p86#2/r3.speaker: مقاتل
WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p86#2/r3.claim: Muqātil adds the doorkeeper's wife to the women named by al-Kalbī.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p86#2/r4.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p86#2/r4.speaker: مجاهد
WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p86#2/r4.claim: Mujāhid gives a similar account of which women were present.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p86#2/r5.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p86#2/r5.speaker: author
WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p86#2/r5.claim: The affair between Joseph and the governor's wife had spread through Egypt, prompting the women of the city to discuss it.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p86#2/r6.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p86#2/r6.speaker: author
WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p86#2/r6.claim: امرأة العزيز means Zulaykhā; in their usage العزيز meant king, and Arabs also call a king العزيز.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p86#2/r7.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p86#2/r7.speaker: أبو دؤاد
WAHIDI-BASIT:v12p86#2/r7.claim: Abū Duʾād's verse uses عزيز for a day of royal power or kingship.

WAHIDI-WAJIZ:12:51-52/r1.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-WAJIZ:12:51-52/r1.speaker: author
WAHIDI-WAJIZ:12:51-52/r1.claim: The king asked all the women together because he did not know which one had tried to seduce Joseph.

WAHIDI-WAJIZ:12:51-52/r2.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-WAJIZ:12:51-52/r2.speaker: author
WAHIDI-WAJIZ:12:51-52/r2.claim: They declared Joseph innocent of adultery or any other evil; the ruler's wife admitted the truth because she feared the women would testify against her.

WAHIDI-WAJIZ:12:51-52/r3.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-WAJIZ:12:51-52/r3.speaker: author
WAHIDI-WAJIZ:12:51-52/r3.claim: The ruler's wife said she had tried to seduce Joseph and that his claim that she initiated it was true.

JISHUMI:v5p3659/r2.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v5p3659/r2.speaker: أبو عمرو
JISHUMI:v5p3659/r2.claim: Abū ʿAmr reads حاشا with a final alif; the other readers omit it.

JISHUMI:v5p3659/r3.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v5p3659/r3.speaker: author
JISHUMI:v5p3659/r3.claim: Khaṭb is a matter of great consequence addressed between people; وما خطبك asks what the matter or situation is.

JISHUMI:v5p3659/r4.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v5p3659/r4.speaker: أبو مسلم
JISHUMI:v5p3659/r4.claim: Abū Muslim says ḥāshā combines exception, declaring someone free of blame, and astonishment; adding it to God's name conveys wonder, like an Arab exclamation asking for help or expressing surprise.

JISHUMI:v5p3659/r5.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v5p3659/r5.speaker: الزجاج
JISHUMI:v5p3659/r5.claim: Al-Zajjāj analyzes ḥaṣḥaṣ as a reduplicated form whose root is ḥaṣṣ, comparable to other doubled forms; ḥaṣṣ means cutting something away completely, so the truth became clear.

JISHUMI:v5p3659/r6.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v5p3659/r6.speaker: author
JISHUMI:v5p3659/r6.claim: Ḥaṣṣ is to cut away completely, and ḥiṣṣa is a portion; the verb ḥaṣḥaṣ can mean becoming clear, with further examples for hair cut short, an egg clearing the head, land stripped of growth, or a camel leaving marks.

JISHUMI:v5p3659/r7.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v5p3659/r7.speaker: حميد
JISHUMI:v5p3659/r7.claim: Ḥumayd's cited line uses ḥaṣḥaṣ for a camel settling its knees against hard stones until their marks show.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v4p248/r1.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v4p248/r1.speaker: author
BAGHAWI-FULL:v4p248/r1.claim: The king addresses all the women but intends the question about seducing Joseph for the Aziz’s wife; alternatively, she alone seduced him and the other women urged her to comply.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v4p248/r2.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v4p248/r2.speaker: author
BAGHAWI-FULL:v4p248/r2.claim: The women’s “God forbid” means they know of no wrongdoing or betrayal by Joseph.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v4p248/r3.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v4p248/r3.speaker: author
BAGHAWI-FULL:v4p248/r3.claim: “Now the truth is clear” may follow the women’s confrontation and confession, or the wife may have confessed from fear they would testify against her.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v4p248/r4.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v4p248/r4.speaker: امرأة العزيز
BAGHAWI-FULL:v4p248/r4.claim: The Aziz’s wife admits she seduced Joseph and confirms that he told the truth about her pursuing him.

KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p450/r10.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p450/r10.speaker: author
KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p450/r10.claim: The passive reading ḥuḥṣiṣa means the truth became established; its form is associated with a camel settling onto its chest.

KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p450/r8.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p450/r8.speaker: author
KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p450/r8.claim: Mā khaṭbukun means what is your affair; Yusuf asks whether the women found any inclination toward them in him.

KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p450/r9.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p450/r9.speaker: author
KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p450/r9.claim: The women say ḥāsha li-llāh to express amazement at Yusuf's chastity, self-respect, and freedom from suspicion.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p253/r1.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p253/r1.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p253/r1.claim: The king assembles the women with the governor’s wife and asks what their affair was when they pursued Joseph.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p253/r2.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p253/r2.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p253/r2.claim: The women’s answer protects their own position and gives Joseph some vindication, but ما علمنا عليه من سوء is not a complete declaration of his innocence.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p253/r3.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p253/r3.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p253/r3.claim: Saying they knew only good about Joseph would have been a stronger exoneration.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p253/r4.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p253/r4.speaker: البخاري
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p253/r4.claim: Bukhari classifies this kind of statement as testimony to a person’s reliability, citing Usama ibn Zayd’s statement in the slander report.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p253/r5.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p253/r5.speaker: مالك
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p253/r5.claim: Malik does not accept such words as sufficient to certify a witness, because they do not establish his moral uprightness.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p253/r6.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p253/r6.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p253/r6.claim: Ḥaṣḥaṣ al-ḥaqq means that the truth became clear after being hidden; another explanation derives it from the separation of one share from another.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p253/r7.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p253/r7.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p253/r7.claim: The governor’s wife admits that she pursued Joseph and fully clears him of blame.

TABRISI:12:51-52/r1.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:12:51-52/r1.speaker: author
TABRISI:12:51-52/r1.claim: Yusuf refuses to leave until the king learns the women's affair and his innocence; he asks about all the women rather than naming the Aziz's wife, out of courtesy to her status or because the women were witnesses against her.

TABRISI:12:51-52/r2.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:12:51-52/r2.speaker: ابن عباس
TABRISI:12:51-52/r2.claim: The Prophet says he would have required release before giving the king his interpretation.

TABRISI:12:51-52/r3.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:12:51-52/r3.speaker: author
TABRISI:12:51-52/r3.claim: The Prophet says he would have hastened to answer the summons and leave prison.

TABRISI:12:51-52/r6.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:12:51-52/r6.speaker: author
TABRISI:12:51-52/r6.claim: The king asks the women what happened when they tried to seduce Yusuf; they declare God free of this and testify that they knew no evil of him.

TABRISI:12:51-52/r7.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:12:51-52/r7.speaker: ابن عباس، مجاهد، قتادة
TABRISI:12:51-52/r7.claim: Al-Hasan's confession that truth is clear means it has become manifest and firmly established; Ibn Abbas, Mujahid, and Qatada are cited.

TABRISI:12:51-52/r8.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:12:51-52/r8.speaker: author
TABRISI:12:51-52/r8.claim: The Aziz's wife admits that she seduced Yusuf and lied in accusing him; her lost hope in him led her to tell the truth, and God thereby removed any remaining doubt about his innocence.

TABRISI:12:51-53/r1.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:12:51-53/r1.speaker: الأعشى، البرجمي
TABRISI:12:51-53/r1.claim: Al-Aʿsha and al-Barjami, transmitting from Abu Bakr from ʿAsim, read النسوة with a ḍamma on the nūn; the rest use kasra, and both are dialect forms.

TABRISI:12:51-53/r2.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:12:51-53/r2.speaker: author
TABRISI:12:51-53/r2.claim: Khaṭb is a serious matter that gives occasion for addressing someone; حصحص الحق may mean truth's share and direction became distinct from falsehood.

TABRISI:12:51-53/r3.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:12:51-53/r3.speaker: author
TABRISI:12:51-53/r3.claim: Another derivation connects حصحص to cutting hair to the skin, so the phrase means truth was separated from falsehood through its disclosure; the source cites poetry and the camel's kneeling marks.

TABRISI:12:51-53/r4.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:12:51-53/r4.speaker: author
TABRISI:12:51-53/r4.claim: Kayd is a stratagem designed to bring harm to another person.

RAZI-FULL:v18p122#2/r1.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v18p122#2/r1.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v18p122#2/r1.claim: The Aziz's wife was present and realized the inquiry concerned her; seeing Joseph had spared her by asking only about the other women, she reciprocated by confessing that all guilt was hers and Joseph was innocent.

RAZI-FULL:v18p122#2/r2.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v18p122#2/r2.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v18p122#2/r2.claim: Al-Razi illustrates reciprocal kindness with a wife who forgives her husband's debt after he spares her embarrassment before witnesses.

RAZI-FULL:v18p122#2/r3.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v18p122#2/r3.speaker: أهل اللغة
RAZI-FULL:v18p122#2/r3.claim: Ḥaṣḥaṣa al-ḥaqq means that truth became clear, emerged, and settled firmly in hearts.

RAZI-FULL:v18p122#2/r4.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v18p122#2/r4.speaker: الزجاج
RAZI-FULL:v18p122#2/r4.claim: Al-Zajjaj derives حصحص from حصّة: the share of truth became distinct from the share of falsehood.

RAZI-FULL:v18p122/r8.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v18p122/r8.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v18p122/r8.claim: The plural question إذ راودتن may address one woman collectively or the whole group; the women may each have pursued Joseph for themselves or on the Aziz's wife's behalf.

RAZI-FULL:v18p122/r9.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v18p122/r9.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v18p122/r9.claim: The women's declaration that they knew no evil of Joseph confirms their earlier praise that he was no ordinary man but a noble angel.

QURTUBI-FULL:12:50-51#2/r1.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:12:50-51#2/r1.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:12:50-51#2/r1.claim: The Prophet's choice to leave immediately and vindicate himself afterward was also sound: people may imitate these stories, and ordinary prisoners cannot know they will safely retain a chance to leave as Joseph did.

QURTUBI-FULL:12:50-51#2/r3.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:12:50-51#2/r3.speaker: ابن عباس
QURTUBI-FULL:12:50-51#2/r3.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās says the king summoned both the women and the Aziz's wife, since the Aziz had died, and asked them what had happened.

QURTUBI-FULL:12:50-51#2/r4.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:12:50-51#2/r4.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:12:50-51#2/r4.claim: Khaṭb means affair or situation; the women either each tried to entice Joseph for herself or each accused the Aziz's wife of wrongdoing, which also amounted to enticement.

QURTUBI-FULL:12:50-51#2/r5.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:12:50-51#2/r5.speaker: قيل
QURTUBI-FULL:12:50-51#2/r5.claim: An alternative reading of the episode is that each woman reproached the Aziz's wife, so their words themselves constituted an enticement of Joseph.

QURTUBI-FULL:12:50-51#2/r6.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:12:50-51#2/r6.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:12:50-51#2/r6.claim: Ḥāsha li-llāh means seeking God's protection, and the women say they know no evil of Joseph, meaning adultery.

QURTUBI-FULL:12:50-51#2/r7.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:12:50-51#2/r7.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:12:50-51#2/r7.claim: The Aziz's wife sees the women admit Joseph's innocence, fears they will testify against her if she denies it, and confesses; this is God's kindness to Joseph.

QURTUBI-FULL:12:50-51#3/r1.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:12:50-51#3/r1.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:12:50-51#3/r1.claim: A cited line about Khudāsh uses ḥaṣḥaṣ al-ḥaqq to mean truth appearing and exposing a liar.

QURTUBI-FULL:12:50-51#3/r2.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:12:50-51#3/r2.speaker: أبو القيس بن الأسلت
QURTUBI-FULL:12:50-51#3/r2.claim: Abū Qays ibn al-Aslat's verse about an egg having shaved his head witnesses ḥaṣṣ as cutting hair down to its root.

QURTUBI-FULL:12:50-51#3/r3.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:12:50-51#3/r3.speaker: جرير
QURTUBI-FULL:12:50-51#3/r3.claim: Jarīr's phrase al-sana al-ḥaṣāʾ describes a barren year; he substitutes wolf for hyena for rhyme, supporting the sense of a stripped or barren year.

QURTUBI-FULL:12:50-51#3/r4.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:12:50-51#3/r4.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:12:50-51#3/r4.claim: On this derivation, the truth has cut through falsehood by appearing and becoming established; the cited line uses ḥaṣḥaṣa for truth's manifestation.

QURTUBI-FULL:12:50-51#3/r5.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:12:50-51#3/r5.speaker: قيل
QURTUBI-FULL:12:50-51#3/r5.claim: Another derivation links the phrase to ḥiṣṣa, meaning the share of truth became distinct from the share of falsehood.

QURTUBI-FULL:12:50-51#3/r6.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:12:50-51#3/r6.speaker: مجاهد
QURTUBI-FULL:12:50-51#3/r6.claim: Mujāhid and Qatāda derive the word from completely cutting hair or cutting off a portion of land; al-Jawharī also defines ḥaṣḥaṣ as gravel and stones.

QURTUBI-FULL:12:50-51#3/r7.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:12:50-51#3/r7.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:12:50-51#3/r7.claim: The wife's unsolicited confession displays repentance and confirms Joseph's truthfulness and honor: self-incrimination is stronger than testimony, so God combines confession with testimony to remove all doubt.

QURTUBI-FULL:12:50-51#3/r8.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:12:50-51#3/r8.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:12:50-51#3/r8.claim: The nūn is geminated in khuṭbikunna and rāwadtunna because it functions like the mīm and wāw endings of masculine plural forms.

QURTUBI-FULL:12:50-51/r10.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:12:50-51/r10.speaker: ابن عطية
QURTUBI-FULL:12:50-51/r10.claim: Ibn ʿAṭiyya explains Joseph's delay as patient insistence on clearing his name before accepting royal favor, lest people forever remember the false accusation; Joseph also avoids offending the Aziz's household and honors the king's trust.

QURTUBI-FULL:12:50-51/r3.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:12:50-51/r3.speaker: أبو هريرة
QURTUBI-FULL:12:50-51/r3.claim: In a report from Abū Hurayra, the Prophet calls Joseph son of four noble generations and says that, had he stayed in prison as long as Joseph, he would have answered the summons; he also recites the request to investigate the women.

QURTUBI-FULL:12:50-51/r4.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:12:50-51/r4.speaker: أبو هريرة
QURTUBI-FULL:12:50-51/r4.claim: Al-Tirmidhī's report from Abū Hurayra also has the Prophet praise Lot for relying on a strong support and say every prophet after him had a position of strength among his people.

QURTUBI-FULL:12:50-51/r5.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:12:50-51/r5.speaker: أبو هريرة
QURTUBI-FULL:12:50-51/r5.claim: Al-Bukhārī's report from Abū Hurayra repeats the prayer for mercy on Lot and the Prophet's statement that he would have answered the summons if imprisoned as long as Joseph; it adds that Abraham's request sought reassurance.

QURTUBI-FULL:12:50-51/r6.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:12:50-51/r6.speaker: النبي
QURTUBI-FULL:12:50-51/r6.claim: A further prophetic report calls Joseph patient and forbearing and says the Prophet would have answered the summons without seeking an excuse.

QURTUBI-FULL:12:50-51/r7.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:12:50-51/r7.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:12:50-51/r7.claim: A similar report comes through ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn al-Qāsim, a companion of Mālik, in al-Bukhārī's tafsir collection; it is his only report there.

QURTUBI-FULL:12:50-51/r8.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:12:50-51/r8.speaker: الطبري
QURTUBI-FULL:12:50-51/r8.claim: Al-Ṭabarī's version says the Prophet would have left quickly if summoned from prison and describes Joseph as forbearing and deliberate.

QURTUBI-FULL:12:50-51/r9.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:12:50-51/r9.speaker: النبي
QURTUBI-FULL:12:50-51/r9.claim: Another report has the Prophet marvel at Joseph's patience in interpreting the cows before securing release, and at his delaying departure when the messenger arrived.

BAYDAWI-FULL:12:51-52/r1.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:12:51-52/r1.speaker: author
BAYDAWI-FULL:12:51-52/r1.claim: The king asks the women about an affair weighty enough to address them over; khatb denotes such a matter.

BAYDAWI-FULL:12:51-52/r2.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:12:51-52/r2.speaker: author
BAYDAWI-FULL:12:51-52/r2.claim: The women exclaim that God is beyond imperfection, marveling at His power to create a man as chaste as Joseph.

BAYDAWI-FULL:12:51-52/r3.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:12:51-52/r3.speaker: author
BAYDAWI-FULL:12:51-52/r3.claim: The queen's حصحص means the truth became established; it may derive from a camel settling onto its knees or hair being removed to expose the scalp.

BAYDAWI-FULL:12:51-52/r4.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:12:51-52/r4.speaker: author
BAYDAWI-FULL:12:51-52/r4.claim: A passive-voice reading of حصحص is also transmitted.

BAYDAWI-FULL:12:51-52/r5.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:12:51-52/r5.speaker: author
BAYDAWI-FULL:12:51-52/r5.claim: The wife of the ruler admits she tried to seduce Joseph and confirms his earlier statement that she pursued him.

NASAFI-FULL:v2p193/r1.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v2p193/r1.speaker: author
NASAFI-FULL:v2p193/r1.claim: The king asks the women whether they felt any inclination from Joseph; their exclamation 'God forbid' expresses amazement that God created someone so chaste.

NASAFI-FULL:v2p193/r2.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v2p193/r2.speaker: author
NASAFI-FULL:v2p193/r2.claim: The women deny any wrongdoing by Joseph; the minister's wife admits the truth has emerged and confirms his statement that she solicited him.

NASAFI-FULL:v2p193/r3.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v2p193/r3.speaker: author
NASAFI-FULL:v2p193/r3.claim: There is no stronger proof of his innocence than their testimony for him and their confession against themselves; the messenger returns with their words and the wife's admission.

QASHANI:12:49-51/r2.author: ʿAbd al-Razzāq al-Qāshānī
QASHANI:12:49-51/r2.speaker: author
QASHANI:12:49-51/r2.claim: The women's acquittal and the ruler's wife's confession symbolize soul and faculties becoming truthful and just through unity; the tranquil soul admits the heart's virtue and its own fault and seeks divine mercy.

QASHANI:12:49-51/r3.author: ʿAbd al-Razzāq al-Qāshānī
QASHANI:12:49-51/r3.speaker: author
QASHANI:12:49-51/r3.claim: Joseph's enthronement and the ruler's death signify the heart's succession to divine stewardship; marriage to the ruler's wife means the tranquil soul receives lawful benefits that support justice and knowledge.

QASHANI:12:49-51/r4.author: ʿAbd al-Razzāq al-Qāshānī
QASHANI:12:49-51/r4.speaker: author
QASHANI:12:49-51/r4.claim: The wife remaining a virgin signifies her balanced tranquility and the spirit's transcendence from the soul; she is the heart's wife because the heart governs her through spirit.

QASHANI:12:49-51/r5.author: ʿAbd al-Razzāq al-Qāshānī
QASHANI:12:49-51/r5.speaker: author
QASHANI:12:49-51/r5.claim: Stewardship signifies the heart's capacity to apprehend and preserve material particulars, unlike the spirit; the Holy Spirit grants this empowerment after annihilation, returning from unity to detail.

QASHANI:12:49-51/r6.author: ʿAbd al-Razzāq al-Qāshānī
QASHANI:12:49-51/r6.speaker: author
QASHANI:12:49-51/r6.claim: The afterlife's reward is spiritual pleasure in witnessing beauty and the lights of the enduring Face, better for those with direct faith who avoid residual selfhood.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p283/r7.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p283/r7.speaker: الخليل
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p283/r7.claim: Al-Khalīl explains ḥaṣḥaṣa as becoming clear after being hidden.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p283/r8.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p283/r8.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p283/r8.claim: Other lexical explanations derive ḥaṣḥaṣ from the share allotted to truth over falsehood, or from a camel settling firmly on its knees.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p283/r9.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p283/r9.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p283/r9.claim: Al-jihāz means travelers' provisions and equipment, anything carried, a bride's trousseau, or what is needed to bury the dead.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p287#2/r11.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p287#2/r11.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p287#2/r11.claim: The king’s question follows an omitted return and report by the messenger; he gathered the women and al-Aziz’s wife to recount the case.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p287#2/r12.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p287#2/r12.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p287#2/r12.claim: The king frames the matter as their solicitation of Joseph; their urging him to obey their mistress was their attempt.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p287#2/r13.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p287#2/r13.speaker: الزمخشري
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p287#2/r13.claim: Al-Zamakhshari reads their exclamation as amazement at Joseph’s chastity and distance from suspicion.

SAMIN-DURR:12:51/r1.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:12:51/r1.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:12:51/r1.claim: خطب means a serious affair; it is the verbal noun of خطب, used for momentous matters.

SAMIN-DURR:12:51/r2.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:12:51/r2.speaker: امرؤ القيس
SAMIN-DURR:12:51/r2.claim: Imru al-Qays uses الخطوب for grave events in the cited line.

SAMIN-DURR:12:51/r3.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:12:51/r3.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:12:51/r3.claim: إذ راودتن is governed by خطبكن, which carries verbal force: what did you do or intend at that time?

SAMIN-DURR:12:51/r4.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:12:51/r4.speaker: الخليل
SAMIN-DURR:12:51/r4.claim: Al-Khalil explains حصحص as becoming clear after being hidden.

SAMIN-DURR:12:51/r5.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:12:51/r5.speaker: بعضهم
SAMIN-DURR:12:51/r5.claim: One derivation relates حصحص to حصة: truth's share became distinct from falsehood's share.

SAMIN-DURR:12:51/r6.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:12:51/r6.speaker: قيل
SAMIN-DURR:12:51/r6.claim: Another gloss is that the truth became established and settled.

SAMIN-DURR:12:51/r7.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:12:51/r7.speaker: الراغب
SAMIN-DURR:12:51/r7.claim: Al-Raghib says حصحص is disclosure after what covers the truth is removed, and compares doubled forms such as كفكف.

SAMIN-DURR:12:51/r8.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:12:51/r8.speaker: الراغب
SAMIN-DURR:12:51/r8.claim: Al-Raghib connects حصه to cutting directly or by judgment; the cited poem has قد حصت for direct cutting.

SAMIN-DURR:12:51/r9.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:12:51/r9.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:12:51/r9.claim: Another derivation is a camel lowering its knee pads to kneel, illustrated by an anonymous verse.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v4p394/r1.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v4p394/r1.speaker: author
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v4p394/r1.claim: The king asks all the women, meaning the Aziz's wife in particular, what happened when they tried to seduce Yusuf; they answer that God forbid, they knew no evil of him.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v4p394/r2.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v4p394/r2.speaker: ابن عباس
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v4p394/r2.claim: Ibn Abbas, Mujahid, and others explain 'now the truth is clear' as the truth having become evident, appeared, and stood out.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v4p394/r3.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v4p394/r3.speaker: author
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v4p394/r3.claim: On the woman's reading of the passage, the Aziz's wife admits she solicited Yusuf and that his claim about her is true; she says she did so to show her husband she did not betray him in fact or commit the greater sin.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v4p394/r5.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v4p394/r5.speaker: author
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v4p394/r5.claim: The most well-known and contextually fitting reading makes these words the Aziz's wife's speech; al-Mawardi reports it and Ibn Taymiyya separately defended it.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v4p395/r2.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v4p395/r2.speaker: author
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v4p395/r2.claim: Ibn Kathir prefers the first, wife-speaker reading because the entire exchange is her speech before the king and Yusuf is absent until afterward.

BIQAI-FULL:v4p57/r1.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v4p57/r1.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v4p57/r1.claim: The king’s question about the women’s serious affair and the wording “when you solicited Joseph” show that his innocence was already recognized, though people were unsure which women had acted.

BIQAI-FULL:v4p57/r2.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v4p57/r2.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v4p57/r2.claim: The women evade the king’s question: “God forbid” and “we knew no evil of him” clear Joseph while leaving their own actions unconfessed.

BIQAI-FULL:v4p57/r3.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v4p57/r3.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v4p57/r3.claim: Their emphatic “no evil” makes Joseph’s innocence comprehensive; the court’s indirect speech also reflects fear of royal authority and a desire to leave room for evasion.

BIQAI-FULL:v4p57/r4.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v4p57/r4.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v4p57/r4.claim: The wife of the ʿAzīz admits that she pursued Joseph and confirms his truthfulness, after all the women have testified that he committed no wrong.

BIQAI-FULL:v4p57/r5.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v4p57/r5.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v4p57/r5.claim: Ḥaṣḥaṣ means the truth has become fully manifest and falsehood has withdrawn; Biqāʿī explains it through intensifying the root ḥ-ṣ-ṣ.

BIQAI-FULL:v4p57/r6.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v4p57/r6.speaker: الزجاج
BIQAI-FULL:v4p57/r6.claim: Al-Zajjāj derives ḥaṣḥaṣ from ḥaṣṣ, cutting hair closely until what lies beneath becomes visible; al-Rummānī and al-Rāzī agree.

BIQAI-FULL:v4p57/r7.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v4p57/r7.speaker: الأزهري
BIQAI-FULL:v4p57/r7.claim: Al-Azharī offers another derivation: a camel’s calluses leave visible marks on the ground when it kneels.

DURR-FULL:v4p503#2/r5.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v4p503#2/r5.speaker: author
DURR-FULL:v4p503#2/r5.claim: The women denied seeing evil from Joseph but said the Aziz's wife had told them she pursued him; the wife then declared that the truth had become clear.

DURR-FULL:v4p504/r2.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v4p504/r2.speaker: author
DURR-FULL:v4p504/r2.claim: The Aziz's wife challenged Joseph over the moment he loosened his trousers; Joseph answered that he did not declare himself innocent.

ALUSI-FULL:v12p259#2/r1.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v12p259#2/r1.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v12p259#2/r1.claim: The grammar and derivation of الآن are disputed: its alif is traced to wāw in أوان or to yā in آن يئين; a proposed original أوان with a deleted alif is rejected because wāw before alif does not normally change, while another analysis compares it to راح/رواح.

ALUSI-FULL:v12p259#2/r10.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v12p259#2/r10.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v12p259#2/r10.claim: The Aziz's wife confesses that she seduced Joseph, not that he seduced her, to confirm his innocence; she may have confessed because denial was useless or because obsessive love made her indifferent to exposure.

ALUSI-FULL:v12p259#2/r2.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v12p259#2/r2.speaker: الزجاج
ALUSI-FULL:v12p259#2/r2.claim: Al-Zajjaj says الآن is built because it contains the meaning of a demonstrative, 'this time'; the objection is that demonstrative pronouns do not take the article.

ALUSI-FULL:v12p259#2/r3.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v12p259#2/r3.speaker: أبو علي
ALUSI-FULL:v12p259#2/r3.claim: Abu Ali says الآن is built because it contains the meaning of the definite lam; Al-Alusi objects that an implied particle's meaning cannot sensibly be expressed by adding that very particle.

ALUSI-FULL:v12p259#2/r4.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v12p259#2/r4.speaker: المبرد وابن السراج والزمخشري
ALUSI-FULL:v12p259#2/r4.claim: Al-Mubarrad, Ibn al-Sarraj, and al-Zamakhshari say الآن is built because it was originally indefinite but has used the article since its first use; Ibn Malik objects that other initially articulated phrases remain inflected, and that mere unusualness does not cause building.

ALUSI-FULL:v12p259#2/r5.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v12p259#2/r5.speaker: ابن مالك
ALUSI-FULL:v12p259#2/r5.claim: Ibn Malik instead attributes building to الآن's fixed, particle-like form: unlike حين and وقت it cannot be dualized, pluralized, or diminished; Abu Hayyan objects to the argument.

ALUSI-FULL:v12p259#2/r6.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v12p259#2/r6.speaker: الفراء
ALUSI-FULL:v12p259#2/r6.claim: Al-Farra says الآن retains the building of the past verb آن, 'the time came'; the objection is that it takes the article, unlike that verb, and can be declined.

ALUSI-FULL:v12p259#2/r7.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v12p259#2/r7.speaker: بعضهم
ALUSI-FULL:v12p259#2/r7.claim: Some grammarians treat الآن as an inflected accusative of time, citing a poetic 'both full from now' with genitive nūn; critics reply that the vowel may be built kasra, and Ibn al-Sa'igh says those deriving it from أوان also treat that form as inflected.

ALUSI-FULL:v12p259#2/r8.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v12p259#2/r8.speaker: السيوطي
ALUSI-FULL:v12p259#2/r8.claim: Al-Suyuti chooses to treat الآن as inflected and accusative in an adverbial role because no valid cause for building it has been established; its use outside that role is unproven.

ALUSI-FULL:v12p259#2/r9.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v12p259#2/r9.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v12p259#2/r9.claim: In this sentence الآن modifies حصحص: truth became clear at the time she spoke.

ALUSI-FULL:v12p259/r1.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v12p259/r1.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v12p259/r1.claim: The king's question is introduced as a continuation: what was the women's affair when they tried to seduce Joseph, and did they find that he inclined toward them? Their answer presupposes his total chastity.

ALUSI-FULL:v12p259/r10.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v12p259/r10.speaker: الراغب
ALUSI-FULL:v12p259/r10.claim: Al-Raghib notes the reduplicated pattern حصحص alongside كفكف and كبكب; a passive reading means truth was set in its proper place.

ALUSI-FULL:v12p259/r11.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v12p259/r11.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v12p259/r11.claim: الآن denotes the current time, either the whole moment when an utterance is made or the part of the present represented here; another verse uses it in 'now God has lightened you'.

ALUSI-FULL:v12p259/r2.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v12p259/r2.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v12p259/r2.claim: The women's حاشا لله expresses their amazement and declares Joseph's purity; the indefinite سوء with extra من emphatically denies every kind of wrongdoing.

ALUSI-FULL:v12p259/r3.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v12p259/r3.speaker: الكشف
ALUSI-FULL:v12p259/r3.claim: Al-Kashf explains that the question first asks whether Joseph felt any inclination, which would be the beginning of his response to their advances; their answer marvels at God's creating such chastity and denies even a trace of misconduct.

ALUSI-FULL:v12p259/r4.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v12p259/r4.speaker: ابن عطية
ALUSI-FULL:v12p259/r4.claim: Ibn Atiyya says the women answer well, clearing themselves fully and giving Joseph some vindication; Al-Alusi says that misses al-Kashf's account of the framing question and their words' limited scope.

ALUSI-FULL:v12p259/r5.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v12p259/r5.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v12p259/r5.claim: The Aziz's wife was present; one report says the women turned to press her, while another says fear that the women would repeat what she said when they cut their hands prompted her to confess.

ALUSI-FULL:v12p259/r6.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v12p259/r6.speaker: الخليل
ALUSI-FULL:v12p259/r6.claim: Al-Khalil derives حصحص الحق from حصّة, a portion: the portion of truth became distinct from falsehood; al-Zajjaj agrees.

ALUSI-FULL:v12p259/r7.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v12p259/r7.speaker: الزجاج
ALUSI-FULL:v12p259/r7.claim: Al-Zajjaj also explains حصحص as separating the share of truth from the share of falsehood.

ALUSI-FULL:v12p259/r8.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v12p259/r8.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v12p259/r8.claim: Another derivation connects حصحص to cropping hair until the scalp appears; a line attributed to a poet describes a shaved head, and this too returns to the sense of becoming visible.

ALUSI-FULL:v12p259/r9.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v12p259/r9.speaker: حميد بن ثور الهلالي
ALUSI-FULL:v12p259/r9.claim: Humayd ibn Thawr al-Hilali uses حصحص for a camel settling its chest on hard rocks, supporting the sense that truth became firm and established.

ALUSI-FULL:v12p260/r1.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v12p260/r1.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v12p260/r1.claim: Two explanations are given for the Aziz wife’s confession: she knew denial would not work after the women testified, or her overwhelming love made her disregard exposure and shame.

ALUSI-FULL:v12p260/r2.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v12p260/r2.speaker: إرشاد العقل السليم
ALUSI-FULL:v12p260/r2.claim: Irshad says she means that the actual truth of the disputed incident and her betrayal have now become clear, not merely the women's limited testimony about Joseph's general innocence; now means the moment of her own statement, making even his adversaries attest to his purity.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v12p289#3/r1.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v12p289#3/r1.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v12p289#3/r1.claim: The king's question to the women is a fresh explanatory scene prompted by the preceding narrative; an omitted return and report by the messenger led the king to summon the women from the banquet.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v12p289#3/r2.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v12p289#3/r2.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v12p289#3/r2.claim: Wooing is attributed to the women collectively because some unidentified women did it, or because the city's rumor wrongly blended supposition that it happened at the banquet.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v12p289#3/r3.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v12p289#3/r3.speaker: قيل
IBNASHUR-FULL:v12p289#3/r3.claim: One explanation derives خطب from the need to address someone with questions about an important matter.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v12p289#3/r4.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v12p289#3/r4.speaker: قيل
IBNASHUR-FULL:v12p289#3/r4.claim: Another explanation connects خطب with a خطبة, a speech about a weighty matter, treating the word as a verbal noun with passive sense.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v12p289#3/r5.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v12p289#3/r5.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v12p289#3/r5.claim: The women's answer is narrated separately as a response, and قالت excludes the Aziz's wife because her separate answer follows.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v12p289#3/r6.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v12p289#3/r6.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v12p289#3/r6.claim: حاش لله emphatically denies and disavows the alleged seduction; Ibn ʿĀshūr notes that its readings were discussed earlier.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v12p289#3/r7.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v12p289#3/r7.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v12p289#3/r7.claim: Their claim that they knew no evil of Yusuf explains the emphatic denial and implicitly denies both their wooing him and his wooing them, since either would be known to them.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v12p289#3/r8.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v12p289#3/r8.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v12p289#3/r8.claim: The women confine their testimony to the king's question and avoid mentioning the wife's earlier confession, perhaps from fear of her or affection for her.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v12p291/r1.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v12p291/r1.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v12p291/r1.claim: The wife was among the women summoned: Yusuf's request for those who cut their hands did not include her, but the king's question about who wooed him did; the text omits this transition concisely.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v12p291/r2.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v12p291/r2.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v12p291/r2.claim: الآن means the present time, as in Q 8:66.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v12p291/r3.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v12p291/r3.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v12p291/r3.claim: حصحص means became established; the truth of Yusuf's innocence became firm with the wife's admission after rumor and uncertainty.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v12p291/r4.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v12p291/r4.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v12p291/r4.claim: The past-tense حصحص can describe the very recent establishment of truth; alternatively it is literal past tense if the truth became established through the women's testimony.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v12p291/r5.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v12p291/r5.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v12p291/r5.claim: Fronting “now” restricts the truth's establishment to this moment, contrasting it with the earlier false accusation; this resolves the king's uncertainty between the two accounts.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v12p291/r6.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v12p291/r6.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v12p291/r6.claim: Fronting أنا makes the confession exclusive: the wife, not the other women, pursued Yusuf; she confesses her own guilt and clears him.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v12p291/r7.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v12p291/r7.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v12p291/r7.claim: She further affirms Yusuf's truth with إن and the emphatic lām in “among the truthful,” a construction also found in Q 6:56.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v12p292/r1.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v12p292/r1.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v12p292/r1.claim: The apparent sequence makes verse 52 the Aziz's wife's speech; the minority view, attributed by Ibn ʿAṭiyya to a group and also to al-Jubbāʾī and al-Māwardī, assigns it to Yusuf.

TABATABAI:12:33-34#2/r1.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:12:33-34#2/r1.speaker: author
TABATABAI:12:33-34#2/r1.claim: Joseph’s later wording that he had not betrayed her in his absence, along with the women’s role in the affair, suggests they invited him toward the wife and shared the story with her.

TABATABAI:12:35/r6.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:12:35/r6.speaker: author
TABATABAI:12:35/r6.claim: Later evidence shows the wife may have misled her husband into doubting Joseph’s innocence; she may have arranged or ordered prison both to protect herself and to punish him into obedience.

TABATABAI:12:50-51/r5.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:12:50-51/r5.speaker: author
TABATABAI:12:50-51/r5.claim: The narrative omits the messenger’s return and the king’s next actions; the king summons the women and asks what happened when they pursued Joseph.

TABATABAI:12:50-51/r6.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:12:50-51/r6.speaker: الراغب
TABATABAI:12:50-51/r6.claim: Al-Raghib defines khatb as a grave matter that draws much discussion, citing the questions to the Samaritan and to the messengers.

TABATABAI:12:50-51/r7.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:12:50-51/r7.speaker: الراغب
TABATABAI:12:50-51/r7.claim: Al-Raghib glosses haṣḥaṣa al-haqq as the truth becoming clear through disclosure, and notes related forms of the root.

TABATABAI:12:51-52/r1.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:12:51-52/r1.speaker: author
TABATABAI:12:51-52/r1.claim: The women’s declaration of God’s transcendence echoes their first reaction to Joseph and attests to his complete chastity and purity, just as they had marveled at his beauty.

TABATABAI:12:51-52/r2.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:12:51-52/r2.speaker: author
TABATABAI:12:51-52/r2.claim: The Aziz’s wife admits that she pursued Joseph and that he told the truth, retracting her accusation and fully clearing him of any reciprocation.

TABATABAI:12:51-52/r3.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:12:51-52/r3.speaker: author
TABATABAI:12:51-52/r3.claim: The testimony uses layered emphasis: an indefinite wrong under negation with min, divine-transcendence language, a restrictive confession, and an emphatic nominal declaration of Joseph’s truthfulness.

TABATABAI:12:51-52/r4.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:12:51-52/r4.speaker: author
TABATABAI:12:51-52/r4.claim: Their statements clear Joseph of every wrong, including indecency, soliciting or responding to seduction, inclination, lying, and slander.

TABATABAI:12:93-102#3/r2.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:12:93-102#3/r2.speaker: بعض الروايات
TABATABAI:12:93-102#3/r2.claim: Several reports say Joseph married the former wife of al-ʿAzīz after the latter died during the famine years; the author says this might be God's reward for her truthful confession, if the report is sound.

ASAD-NOTES:12:50#n49/r1.author: Muhammad Asad
ASAD-NOTES:12:50#n49/r1.speaker: author
ASAD-NOTES:12:50#n49/r1.claim: The King investigates whether the women had previously been encouraged by Joseph; khatb means what someone has in view, desires, or seeks to obtain.

ASAD-NOTES:12:50#n50/r1.author: Muhammad Asad
ASAD-NOTES:12:50#n50/r1.speaker: author
ASAD-NOTES:12:50#n50/r1.claim: Al-aziz literally means the great one in the phrase for the wife of Joseph's former master.

ASAD-NOTES:12:50#n51/r1.author: Muhammad Asad
ASAD-NOTES:12:50#n51/r1.speaker: Ibn Kathir, Rashid Rida'
ASAD-NOTES:12:50#n51/r1.claim: Ibn Kathir and Rashid Rida' read the following verses as continuing the woman's confession; Asad rejects this attribution.

ASAD-NOTES:12:50#n51/r2.author: Muhammad Asad
ASAD-NOTES:12:50#n51/r2.speaker: Tabari, Baghawi, Zamakhshari
ASAD-NOTES:12:50#n51/r2.claim: The majority of classical authorities assign the following speech to Joseph, rather than continuing the woman's confession.

ASAD-NOTES:12:50#n51/r3.author: Muhammad Asad
ASAD-NOTES:12:50#n51/r3.speaker: author
ASAD-NOTES:12:50#n51/r3.claim: Asad favors the classical attribution to Joseph as the most convincing reading and says it motivates his interpolation.

ASAD-NOTES:12:50#n52/r1.author: Muhammad Asad
ASAD-NOTES:12:50#n52/r1.speaker: author
ASAD-NOTES:12:50#n52/r1.claim: Bi'l-ghayb means in his absence or in secret.

ASAD-NOTES:12:intro/r2.author: Muhammad Asad
ASAD-NOTES:12:intro/r2.speaker: author
ASAD-NOTES:12:intro/r2.claim: Unlike Genesis' romantic account of Joseph's fortunes, the Qur'anic story illustrates God's unfathomable direction of human affairs: people may hate what is good for them or love what is bad for them.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-4-surah-yunus-10-sur.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-4-surah-yunus-10-sur.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-4-surah-yunus-10-sur.claim: Joseph's patience left no room for accusation, so the women openly admitted finding no evil desire in him.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-4-surah-yunus-10-sur.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-4-surah-yunus-10-sur.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-4-surah-yunus-10-sur.claim: The wife of Aziz went further than the other women in confessing the truth.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-4-surah-yunus-10-sur.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-4-surah-yunus-10-sur.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-4-surah-yunus-10-sur.claim: The king summoned the women after receiving Joseph's request, and his wording shows he already believed Joseph innocent and the women deceptive.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-4-surah-yunus-10-sur.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-4-surah-yunus-10-sur.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-4-surah-yunus-10-sur.claim: Had the king been unsure, he would have asked neutrally what had happened between the women and Joseph.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-4-surah-yunus-10-sur.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-4-surah-yunus-10-sur.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-4-surah-yunus-10-sur.claim: Truth becomes manifest through patience, until circumstances and even enemies testify to the truthful person's veracity.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-4-surah-yunus-10-sur.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-4-surah-yunus-10-sur.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-4-surah-yunus-10-sur.claim: The expressions ḥāshā and ḥāsha are used to clear someone of blame.

KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:12:51/r1.author: Hayreddin Karaman, Mustafa Çağrıcı, İbrahim Kâfi Dönmez, Sadrettin Gümüş
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:12:51/r1.speaker: author
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:12:51/r1.claim: The king likely knew the case and believed Joseph innocent but had tolerated injustice to protect officials’ standing; when questioned, the women admitted Joseph’s innocence and Aziz’s wife confessed the truth.

QIRAAT-ER:12:51:10#1/r1.author: QIRAAT-ER
QIRAAT-ER:12:51:10#1/r1.speaker: author
QIRAAT-ER:12:51:10#1/r1.claim: The standard recitation has no final alif.

QIRAAT-ER:12:51:10#2/r1.author: QIRAAT-ER
QIRAAT-ER:12:51:10#2/r1.speaker: author
QIRAAT-ER:12:51:10#2/r1.claim: The variant with long final ā is canonical and makes the form more like a full verb.

STUDYQURAN:12:51/r1.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:12:51/r1.speaker: Kl
STUDYQURAN:12:51/r1.claim: The women’s denial of knowing evil against Joseph absolved him of blame.

STUDYQURAN:12:51/r2.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:12:51/r2.speaker: My
STUDYQURAN:12:51/r2.claim: Some commentators say Zulaykhā’s love had surpassed self-interest, leading her to tell the truth about Joseph.

STUDYQURAN:12:51/r3.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:12:51/r3.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:12:51/r3.claim: Earlier Zulaykhā falsely blamed Joseph because her desire mattered more to her than his well-being.

STUDYQURAN:12:51/r4.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:12:51/r4.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:12:51/r4.claim: Later she admitted his innocence only to a small group of women to protect herself from their scorn.

STUDYQURAN:12:51/r5.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:12:51/r5.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:12:51/r5.claim: The narrative presents Zulaykhā’s spiritual development as a progression from sensual attraction to love that recognizes Joseph’s inward beauty.

STUDYQURAN:12:51/r6.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:12:51/r6.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:12:51/r6.claim: Her spiritual love for Joseph’s inward beauty parallels Potiphar’s earlier recognition of it in the marketplace.

STUDYQURAN:12:51/r7.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:12:51/r7.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:12:51/r7.claim: Joseph’s inner virtue, especially truthfulness, catalyzed this change, and Zulaykhā recognized it in calling him truthful.
